name: Databases in Practice
author: Recurse
subject: swe
description: Model data, normalize to 3NF, index and EXPLAIN queries, use transactions safely, avoid N+1 and SQL injection, pick SQL or NoSQL.

lesson.intro: Real work asks more than SQL basics: tables that stay correct as the app grows, a fast query on 40 million rows, consistent money when two requests race, and an ORM that quietly runs 500 queries. These are the database skills interns pick up first.
objectives: Design tables with keys and junction tables, normalized to 3NF
Explain how a B-tree index helps, when it hurts, and composite column order
Read an EXPLAIN plan well enough to spot a missing index
Use transactions and recognize isolation anomalies and lost updates
Prevent N+1 queries and SQL injection, and justify SQL or NoSQL

sections.title: Modeling data: tables, keys and relationships
sections.key: Give every table a stable primary key, put the foreign key on the many side of a one-to-many, and model many-to-many with a junction table.
sections.body:
You are building a course platform: teachers write courses, students enroll, and you track when. Decide the tables and how they point at each other before writing a query; a bad schema makes every feature a fight.

[[visual]]

Prefer a **surrogate key**, an auto-generated `id` with no business meaning, over a **natural key** such as an email: emails change, and other tables point at the key.

A **foreign key** constraint makes the database refuse a course whose teacher does not exist. It also decides what happens when the parent row is deleted:

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

visual.title: Relationship shapes
rows: One-to-many: a teacher writes many courses
A foreign key on the many side: `courses.teacher_id`. Never a list of ids on the one side
A **junction table** `enrollments(student_id, course_id)`, also home to facts like `enrolled_at`
A unique foreign key; usually one entity split for size or privacy

visual.title: ON DELETE choices
rows: The children go too: delete a course and its enrollments go with it
Refused while children exist: a teacher with courses stays
The child stays and its link is cleared
visual.caption: Cascades chain: a cascade from teachers to courses, and from courses to enrollments, deletes all three levels.

sections.code:
CREATE TABLE courses (
  id         BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  title      TEXT NOT NULL,
  teacher_id BIGINT NOT NULL
    REFERENCES teachers(id)
    ON DELETE RESTRICT
);

-- many-to-many: one row per pair
CREATE TABLE enrollments (
  student_id  BIGINT NOT NULL
    REFERENCES students(id)
    ON DELETE CASCADE,
  course_id   BIGINT NOT NULL
    REFERENCES courses(id)
    ON DELETE CASCADE,
  enrolled_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL
    DEFAULT now(),
  -- no duplicate enrollments
  PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id)
);
sections.tip: Add NOT NULL, UNIQUE and foreign key constraints from day one. The database enforcing a rule beats every service remembering to check it.
sections.pitfall: Storing a comma-separated list of ids in one column (`course_ids = '3,7,12'`). You cannot join on it, index it or enforce it. Use a junction table.

activity.title: Build the tables yourself
activity.prompt: Create a many-to-many wishlist table and a reviews table with constraints. Check runs test inserts against your tables: duplicates, missing values and ids that do not exist must be rejected.
activity.goal: Both tables pass every test insert.

check.question: Students take many courses and each course has many students. Where do the links between them belong?
choices: In a course_ids column on students holding a comma-separated list
In a student_ids array column on courses
In a junction table enrollments(student_id, course_id) with a foreign key to each side
In a copy of each course row for every enrolled student
check.explanation: Many-to-many relationships need a junction table, one row per pair. Lists in a column cannot be joined, indexed or enforced, and copying course rows duplicates every course fact.

sections.title: Normalization to 3NF in plain words
sections.key: Normalize so each fact lives in exactly one place: every non-key column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.
sections.body:
A hurried teammate built this `orders` table:

[[visual]]

When Dana changes her email, every one of her orders must change, and missing one makes the data disagree: an **update anomaly**. You cannot store a customer before they order (**insertion anomaly**), and deleting Lee's only order forgets Lee (**deletion anomaly**). The cause is one fact stored in many places. **Normalization** splits tables so each fact lives once.

[[visual 2]]

The fix: `customers`, `orders`, `products` and `order_items(order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price_cents)`. The line's unit price records what the customer paid, a different fact.

**Denormalize** (copy a value, keep a count) only for a measured need, with a plan to keep the copies in sync.

visual.title: orders, not normalized
visual.caption: Dana's name and email are stored twice; so is the mug's price.

visual.title: The first three normal forms
rows: One value per cell; repeating things become rows. Broken by `items = 'mug, tee'` or `item1, item2, item3`
Non-key columns depend on the **whole** key (it matters for composite keys). Broken by `product_name` in `order_items(order_id, product_id, ...)`, which depends on product_id alone
Non-key columns depend on **nothing but** the key. Broken by `customer_email`, which depends on `customer_id`: a **transitive dependency**

sections.tip: When the same value is typed into many rows, ask: if this changes, how many rows must I update? More than one is a smell.
sections.pitfall: Treating normalization as "split everything, always". Historical facts such as the price paid or the shipping address are copied at the time of the event, because they must not change later.

check.question: In `employees(emp_id PRIMARY KEY, name, dept_id, dept_name)`, which normal form is violated, and why?
choices: 1NF, because the name column holds two words
3NF, because dept_name depends on dept_id rather than directly on the key
2NF, because the primary key has two columns
None, the table is fully normalized
check.explanation: dept_name depends on dept_id, a non-key column, which is a transitive dependency. Rename a department and you must update every employee in it. The key is a single column, so 2NF cannot be the issue, and a two-word name is still one value.

sections.title: Joins, recapped with the traps
sections.key: Three join traps: find missing matches with a LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL, filter the right table in ON rather than WHERE, and aggregate child tables before joining them.
sections.body:
Your manager asks: "Which March sign-ups never ordered?" and "Paid revenue per customer, including people who spent nothing?" Both are joins, each with a classic trap.

Recap: **INNER JOIN** keeps matched pairs; **LEFT JOIN** keeps every left row, with NULLs where nothing matched.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

[[code]]

visual.title: The three traps
rows: Finding rows with no match: an INNER JOIN never shows them
LEFT JOIN, then `WHERE o.id IS NULL` (an **anti-join**; test a column never NULL in a real match), or `NOT EXISTS`
`WHERE o.status = 'paid'` on a LEFT JOIN drops the NULL rows, so it becomes an inner join
Put conditions on the right-hand table in `ON`
**Fan-out**: joining a row to many multiplies it
Aggregate each child table separately (a subquery or CTE), then join the totals

visual.title: Fan-out: order 7 joined to 3 items and 1 payment
visual.caption: `SUM(p.amount_cents)` now reports 9000 for a single 3000 payment.

sections.code:
-- March sign-ups who never ordered
SELECT c.id, c.email
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.created_at >= '2026-03-01'
  AND c.created_at < '2026-04-01'
  AND o.id IS NULL;

-- paid revenue, keeping zero spenders
SELECT c.id,
  COALESCE(SUM(o.total_cents), 0) AS revenue
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id
 AND o.status = 'paid'   -- in ON, not WHERE
GROUP BY c.id
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
sections.tip: Sanity-check joins with row counts. If `SELECT COUNT(*)` after a join is bigger than you expected, you have fan-out.
sections.pitfall: Putting a condition on the right-hand table of a LEFT JOIN in the WHERE clause, which quietly drops every unmatched row.

activity.title: Spring the join traps
activity.prompt: Revenue that keeps the customers who spent nothing, customers who never ordered, and every employee next to their manager. Each one hides a trap from this section.

check.question: In `customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id`, which WHERE clause keeps only customers who have no orders?
choices: WHERE o.id = NULL
WHERE c.id IS NULL
WHERE o.id IS NULL
WHERE o.customer_id <> c.id
check.explanation: Unmatched customers get NULL in every orders column, and o.id is never NULL for a real order. `= NULL` is never true in SQL, since comparisons with NULL are unknown, so you must use IS NULL.

sections.title: Indexes: how they work and when they hurt
sections.key: A B-tree index turns a full scan into a few page reads for equality, ranges and sorts, costs every write, and a composite index serves only its leftmost columns.
sections.body:
The orders page takes 30 ms on your laptop and 9 seconds in production with 40 million rows. `WHERE customer_id = 42` reads every row: a **full table scan** (PostgreSQL says sequential scan).

An **index** is a separate sorted structure mapping values to rows. The default **B-tree** holds hundreds of keys per node, so 100 million rows need 3 or 4 levels: O(log n), not O(n). Sorted keys also serve ranges and `ORDER BY`.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

A **composite index** sorts by its first column, then the second, like a phone book. **Leftmost prefix rule**: `(customer_id, created_at)` serves `customer_id = 42`, with or without a date range, but generally not a date range alone. Put equality columns first, range or sort columns last.

[[code]]

visual.title: Rows checked to find 48 orders among 40 million
When an index does not help
rows: Each INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE must update every index, and indexes take disk and memory
`is_active` is true for 95% of rows: scanning is cheaper
`WHERE LOWER(email) = ...` cannot use an index on email. Index `LOWER(email)`, or compare the raw column
`LIKE '%son'`: the tree is sorted by the first characters

sections.code:
-- PostgreSQL does not index foreign keys
-- for you: do it yourself
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer
  ON orders (customer_id);

-- equality first, range or sort last
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_created
  ON orders (customer_id, created_at);

-- filter and sort both come from it
SELECT id, total_cents, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;

-- for case-insensitive lookups
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email_lower
  ON users (LOWER(email));
sections.deeper:
Primary keys and UNIQUE constraints get an index automatically. Once the composite index on `(customer_id, created_at)` exists, the single-column index on `customer_id` is redundant, because the composite serves that filter too.

A few databases can "skip scan" a composite index when the first column is missing from the query, but do not count on it: a phone book sorted by last name cannot find everyone named Sam.

MySQL's `WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2026` has the same problem as LOWER(): compare a range on the raw column instead.
sections.tip: Index the columns in the WHERE, JOIN ... ON and ORDER BY clauses of your most frequent slow queries, then confirm with EXPLAIN that the index is used.
sections.pitfall: Adding an index on every column "just in case". Writes slow down, storage grows, and the planner ignores most of them anyway.

check.question: There is an index on `orders(customer_id, created_at)`. Which query can use it least effectively?
choices: WHERE customer_id = 42
WHERE customer_id = 42 AND created_at >= '2026-01-01'
WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC
WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01'
check.explanation: The index is sorted by customer_id first, so a filter on created_at alone has no leftmost column to start from, like searching a phone book by first name. The other three all start with customer_id.

sections.title: Reading query plans with EXPLAIN
sections.key: `EXPLAIN` shows the plan the database chose and `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` actually runs the query with real timings; a sequential scan that discards most rows signals a missing index.
sections.body:
You added an index, but the page is still slow. Did the database use it? Ask instead of guessing.

`EXPLAIN` shows the **query plan**, the steps the planner chose with estimated costs and rows, without running the query. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` **really runs it** and adds actual timings. Read from the most indented line outward.

[[visual]]

[[code]]

The planner is cost-based: on a tiny table, or when most rows match, a sequential scan really is cheaper, so it may skip your index on purpose.

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: What to look for
rows: `Seq Scan` (MySQL: `type: ALL`) on a big table, filter removing most rows
Every needed column was in the index; the table was barely touched
A big `Sort`, or a `Nested Loop` scanning its inner side over and over

steps.label: Capture the exact slow query and typical parameters
Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on production-sized data
Find the expensive step
steps.detail: Such as a Seq Scan that discards most rows

steps.label: Add or change an index matching the filter and sort
Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE again and compare
steps.detail: Paste the before and after into the pull request

sections.code:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;

-- Before: no index on customer_id
-- Seq Scan on orders
--   (actual time=0.031..95.112
--    rows=48 loops=1)
--   Filter: (customer_id = 42)
--   Rows Removed by Filter: 999952
-- Execution Time: 95.140 ms

-- After CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer:
-- Index Scan using idx_orders_customer
--   on orders
--   (actual time=0.020..0.064
--    rows=48 loops=1)
--   Index Cond: (customer_id = 42)
-- Execution Time: 0.081 ms
sections.tip: Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on production-sized data. A plan from a 100-row development table tells you almost nothing.
sections.pitfall: Running `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on an UPDATE or DELETE in production. ANALYZE really executes it, so the rows really change; wrap it in `BEGIN; ... ROLLBACK;`.

check.question: A plan shows `Seq Scan on orders` with `Rows Removed by Filter: 999952` to return 48 rows. What is the most likely fix?
choices: Add an index on the column in the filter
Increase the query's LIMIT
Change SELECT to SELECT DISTINCT
Rewrite the query as a LEFT JOIN
check.explanation: Reading a million rows and discarding nearly all of them is the classic sign of a missing index on the filtered column. LIMIT, DISTINCT and join style do not change how the rows are found.

sections.title: Transactions, ACID and isolation
sections.key: A transaction makes statements succeed or fail as one unit; isolation levels trade anomalies for speed, and lost updates need an atomic UPDATE or a row lock.
sections.body:
Moving $50 from Ana to Ben is two updates. If the server crashes between them, $50 vanishes. A **transaction** makes them one unit:

[[code]]

[[visual]]

Full isolation is expensive, so databases default to something weaker and some anomalies leak through:

[[visual 2]]

[[visual 3]]

To stop lost updates, let the database do the arithmetic in one statement (`SET balance = balance - 30 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 30`), or lock the row with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`.

visual.title: ACID
rows: All statements take effect, or none do; a crash or ROLLBACK undoes partial work
Constraints (foreign keys, CHECK, UNIQUE) hold after every commit
Concurrent transactions do not see each other's unfinished work
Once COMMIT returns, the change survives a crash: it was logged to disk first

visual.title: Concurrency anomalies
rows: You read another transaction's change before it commits, and it then rolls back
You read the same row twice and get two different committed values
You rerun a range query and newly inserted rows appear
Two read-modify-write cycles (both read 100, both write 70) overwrite each other

visual.title: Isolation levels
rows: READ COMMITTED (default in PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server)
Dirty reads. Non-repeatable reads and phantoms can still happen
Results as if transactions ran one at a time; more aborts your code must retry

sections.code:
BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 50
WHERE id = 1;   -- Ana
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 50
WHERE id = 2;   -- Ben
COMMIT;         -- both, permanently

-- something went wrong instead? undo both:
-- ROLLBACK;
sections.deeper:
If the server crashes before COMMIT, recovery rolls the uncommitted transaction back, so neither balance has changed.

Higher isolation levels mean more locking, or more transactions aborted with serialization errors that your code must catch and retry. The SQL standard lets REPEATABLE READ allow phantoms; PostgreSQL's implementation prevents them too.
sections.tip: Keep transactions short. Never wait on a user, an email server or a slow API while holding one open, because the rows it locked stay locked.
sections.pitfall: Read-modify-write in application code (read the balance, subtract in Python, write it back) with no lock and no atomic UPDATE. Under concurrent requests, updates get lost.

activity.title: Commit and roll back
activity.prompt: Move money between two accounts inside one transaction, then rescue a teammate whose UPDATE with no WHERE is still uncommitted.

check.question: The transfer subtracts $50 from Ana, then the server crashes before adding it to Ben. Both updates were in one transaction that never committed. What happens?
choices: Ana has lost $50 and Ben has received nothing
On recovery the uncommitted change is rolled back, so neither balance has changed
The database finishes the second update automatically after restarting
Ben receives $50, but Ana is never charged
check.explanation: Atomicity: an uncommitted transaction is undone as a whole. The database never applies half of it, and it does not try to finish your work for you either.

sections.title: From application code: N+1 queries and SQL injection
sections.key: An ORM can hide one query per item in a loop, the N+1 problem, so eager-load related rows; and send values as parameters so input can never become SQL.
sections.body:
Most database bugs at work hide in the code that builds SQL for you.

**N+1 queries.** An ORM lets you write `order.customer.name` as if it were in memory, but each access can hide a query. A loop over 50 orders runs 51 queries: fast in development with five orders, seconds in production.

[[code]]

Load related rows up front, with one JOIN or one `WHERE id IN (...)`:

[[visual]]

**SQL injection.** `f"... WHERE email = '{email}'"` with input `' OR '1'='1` makes the WHERE always true. **Parameterized queries** send the SQL and the values separately, so values are never parsed as SQL: `?` in sqlite3, `%s` in psycopg, `$1` in node-postgres.

Placeholders carry values only, never table or column names: map a user's sort choice through an allowlist.

visual.title: Eager loading
rows: `select_related` for foreign keys (a JOIN); `prefetch_related` for many-related sets (a second query)

sections.code:
# N+1: 1 query, then 1 per order
paid = Order.objects.filter(status="paid")
for order in paid[:50]:
    # a hidden SELECT on every pass
    print(order.customer.name)

# fixed: one query with a JOIN
rows = paid.select_related("customer")[:50]

# injection: input becomes SQL. Never.
sql = f"SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = '{email}'"
cur.execute(sql)

# parameterized: SQL and value sent apart
cur.execute(
    "SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = ?",
    (email,),  # sqlite3; psycopg uses %s
)
sections.deeper:
`%s` in psycopg is a placeholder, not Python string formatting: you still pass the values as a separate tuple. ORMs parameterize for you, until someone drops into raw SQL with an f-string.

An allowlist for user-chosen sorting looks like `{"newest": "created_at DESC", "price": "price_cents ASC"}`: the user picks a key, and only your own text reaches the query.
sections.tip: Count queries per request in development (Django Debug Toolbar, SQLAlchemy echo, your ORM's query log). A count that grows with the rows on the page is N+1.
sections.pitfall: Escaping quotes by hand or "sanitizing" input with replace(). Attackers know more tricks than your filter; parameters make the problem disappear.

check.question: Why does a parameterized query stop SQL injection?
choices: It strips quote characters from user input before the query runs
It runs every query as a read-only database user
It encrypts the user input before sending it to the database
The SQL text and the values are sent separately, so values are never parsed as SQL
check.explanation: The database parses the query with placeholders first and treats bound values purely as data. Stripping quotes is a fragile filter, and encryption or read-only users do not change how the SQL is parsed.

sections.title: SQL vs NoSQL: choosing a store
sections.key: Choose a store by access pattern: relational for related data with rules, documents for self-contained records that vary in shape, key-value for fast lookups by key.
sections.body:
A teammate wants MongoDB "because it scales"; another wants PostgreSQL "because it's safe". Neither is an argument. Ask: what does the data look like, and how is it read and written?

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

A sensible default for a new product: start with PostgreSQL, add Redis for caching and sessions when you need it, and reach for a document or wide-column store when a specific access pattern or scale demands it. Many systems use several stores, each for what it does best.

items.title: Relational
points: Constraints, foreign keys, multi-row ACID transactions
Scales further than its reputation; PostgreSQL can index JSON

items.title: Document
points: JSON-like documents that nest related data
One fetch reads a whole record
Shared data gets duplicated; cross-document rules are up to you

items.title: Key-value
points: Given a key, return the value, fast
TTLs expire entries on their own
No ad hoc queries across values

visual.title: Need and good fit
rows: Self-contained records that vary in shape: product catalog, CMS content
Huge-scale lookups by a known key

sections.tip: In interviews, justify a database by access pattern: "we always fetch a whole profile by user id" favors key-value or documents; "reports joining orders and refunds" favors SQL.
sections.pitfall: Choosing NoSQL "for scale" when the data is relational and small. You give up joins, constraints and easy transactions to solve a problem you do not have.

check.question: Which is the best fit for user sessions that expire after 30 minutes and are read on every request?
choices: A key-value store such as Redis, with a TTL on each session key
A relational table joined with three others on every request
One large document holding every user's session
Flat files stored on each web server's disk
check.explanation: Sessions are looked up by a single key on every request and expire on a timer, which is exactly what a key-value store with TTLs does best. Files on one web server also break as soon as you run two servers.

keyTerms.definition: A column or set of columns that uniquely identifies each row and never changes.
A column holding another table's primary key, with a constraint the database enforces.
A table with one row per pair, linking two tables in a many-to-many relationship.
Splitting tables so each fact is stored once, avoiding update, insert and delete anomalies.
Every non-key column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.
A balanced, sorted tree of keys that finds rows in O(log n) and serves ranges and ORDER BY.
A composite index helps queries that filter on its first column, or first columns, in order.
The steps the database chose to run a query, shown by EXPLAIN; EXPLAIN ANALYZE adds real timings.
A group of statements that commit together or roll back together.
How much concurrent transactions can see of each other; READ COMMITTED is a common default.
One query for a list plus one more for each item, usually from lazy loading in an ORM.
SQL sent with placeholders and the values separately, so input is never parsed as SQL.

summary: Stable primary keys, enforced foreign keys, junction tables for many-to-many.
Each fact in one place: the key, the whole key, nothing but the key.
B-trees serve equality, ranges and sorts but cost writes; composite indexes follow the leftmost prefix.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE before and after a fix, and remember it really runs the statement.
Transactions are atomic; prevent lost updates with atomic UPDATEs or row locks.
Eager-load, parameterize, and pick stores by access pattern.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a junior teammate why a query on a 40-million-row table is slow, how a B-tree index fixes it, and why you should not simply index every column.

questions.question: Each blog post has one author, and an author writes many posts. Where does the foreign key go?
choices: authors.post_ids, holding a list of post ids
A separate table for each author's posts
authors.post_id, referencing posts(id)
posts.author_id, referencing authors(id)
questions.explanation: In a one-to-many relationship the foreign key goes on the 'many' side: each post row points at its author. A list of post ids on authors cannot be joined or enforced.

questions.question: Why do most teams give the users table a surrogate `id` primary key instead of using the email address as the key?
choices: Email columns cannot be indexed
Emails can change, and a primary key that other tables reference should never change
SQL requires every primary key to be an integer
UNIQUE constraints do not work on text columns
questions.explanation: Primary keys are copied into every table that references them, so they should never change. Emails do change, and updating a key everywhere it is referenced is painful and risky. Emails can be indexed and kept UNIQUE just fine.

questions.question: With the constraints below, an admin deletes teacher 5, who has two courses with 40 enrollments between them. What happens?
choices: Only the teacher row is deleted, and the courses keep teacher_id 5
The teacher, both courses and all 40 enrollments are deleted
The delete fails because courses still reference the teacher
The courses stay, with teacher_id set to NULL
questions.explanation: The cascade chains: deleting the teacher deletes their courses, and deleting each course deletes its enrollments. With RESTRICT on courses.teacher_id the delete would have been refused instead.

questions.question: Using this table design, Dana changes her email address. What problem does the design cause?
choices: Her past orders are deleted automatically
The table can no longer be filtered by customer_id
Every one of her order rows must be updated, and missing one leaves the data inconsistent
The new email is rejected by the primary key
questions.explanation: Dana's email is copied into every one of her orders. Changing it means updating many rows, and missing any leaves the data contradicting itself. That is an update anomaly, fixed by moving customer facts into a customers table.

questions.question: `order_items(order_id, product_id, quantity, product_name)` has the primary key (order_id, product_id). Which normal form does it violate?
choices: 1NF, because quantity and product_name are different types
2NF, because product_name depends on only part of the composite key
None, because the key has two columns
Only 1NF, because order_id is repeated across rows
questions.explanation: product_name depends only on product_id, which is just part of the composite key. That partial dependency breaks 2NF (and therefore 3NF too). quantity is fine, because it depends on the whole key: this product in this order.

questions.question: State the rule for third normal form in plain words.
questions.answer: Every non-key column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key. No column depends on part of a composite key or on another non-key column, so each fact is stored in exactly one place.
questions.explanation: This is the line to remember in interviews: each fact lives in one place, so updates touch one row.

questions.question: Complete the query so it returns customers who have never placed an order.
questions.code:
SELECT c.id, c.email
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id _____;
choices: = NULL
IS NOT NULL
IS NULL
<> c.id
questions.explanation: Unmatched customers get NULLs for every orders column, and IS NULL is the only way to test for NULL. `= NULL` is never true, and IS NOT NULL would return customers who do have orders.

questions.question: Given these tables, how many rows does `SELECT * FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id` return?
questions.explanation: Ana matches two orders (2 rows), Ben matches one (1 row) and Cy matches none but is kept with NULLs (1 row): 4 in total. Order 104 points at customer 9, who is not in customers, so a LEFT JOIN from customers never shows it.

questions.question: Order 7 has 3 items and a single payment of 3000 cents. What does this query report as `paid` for order 7?
questions.code:
SELECT o.id, SUM(p.amount_cents) AS paid
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN payments p    ON p.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY o.id;
choices: 3000, because SUM ignores duplicate rows
1000, because the payment is split across the items
An error, because two joins cannot share one GROUP BY
9000, because the payment row is repeated once per item
questions.explanation: Joining order 7 to its 3 items produces 3 rows, and the payment is joined onto each one, so SUM adds 3000 three times. Aggregate payments in their own subquery, then join the total.

questions.question: The goal is every customer with their count of paid orders, showing 0 for customers with none. Customers without paid orders are missing. Why?
questions.code:
SELECT c.id, COUNT(o.id) AS paid_orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY c.id;
choices: The WHERE condition on o.status removes the rows where o is NULL, turning the LEFT JOIN into an inner join
COUNT(o.id) should be COUNT(*)
GROUP BY must also include o.status
A LEFT JOIN never returns rows without a match
questions.explanation: For customers with no matching order, o.status is NULL, and `NULL = 'paid'` is not true, so WHERE removes them and the LEFT JOIN behaves like an INNER JOIN. Move the condition into the ON clause. COUNT(*) would make it worse, counting 1 for customers with no orders.

questions.question: What do you trade when you add an index to a table?
choices: Faster writes in exchange for slower reads
Faster reads on the indexed columns in exchange for slower writes and extra storage
Less storage in exchange for slower reads
Nothing, because indexes are maintained for free
questions.explanation: Indexes speed up reads that filter, join or sort on the indexed columns, but every write must also update the index, and the index takes disk and memory.

questions.question: The table has 5 million users, and this query still scans all of them. Why is the index not used?
questions.code:
CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users (email);

SELECT id FROM users WHERE LOWER(email) = 'dana@example.com';
choices: B-tree indexes do not work on text columns
The query needs LIMIT 1 before an index can be used
The index must be rebuilt after every insert
LOWER() is applied to the column, so its values no longer match the index; index LOWER(email) instead
questions.explanation: The index stores email values as written, sorted. LOWER(email) produces different values the index knows nothing about, so the database must compute it for every row. Index the expression LOWER(email), or store emails lowercased and compare directly.

questions.question: There is a B-tree index on `users(last_name)`. Which of these can use it to avoid scanning the whole table? Select all that apply.
choices: WHERE last_name = 'Smith'
WHERE last_name LIKE '%ith'
WHERE last_name BETWEEN 'Adams' AND 'Baker'
WHERE UPPER(last_name) = 'SMITH'
ORDER BY last_name LIMIT 10
WHERE first_name = 'Sam'
questions.explanation: Equality, ranges and ordering on the indexed column all follow the sorted tree. A leading wildcard, a function around the column, or a filter on a different column cannot use it.

questions.question: Type the SQL statement that creates an index named idx_orders_customer on the customer_id column of the orders table.
accept: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders (customer_id)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders (customer_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders(customer_id)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders(customer_id);
questions.explanation: CREATE INDEX name ON table (columns). In PostgreSQL, foreign key columns such as customer_id are not indexed automatically, so this is one of the most common indexes you will add.

questions.question: This query runs thousands of times a minute: `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20`. Type the statement that creates a composite index named idx_orders_cust_created that serves both the filter and the sort.
questions.answer: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_created ON orders (customer_id, created_at);
accept: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_created ON orders (customer_id, created_at)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_created ON orders (customer_id, created_at);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_created ON orders (customer_id,created_at)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_created ON orders (customer_id,created_at);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_created ON orders(customer_id, created_at)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_created ON orders(customer_id, created_at);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_created ON orders(customer_id,created_at)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_created ON orders(customer_id,created_at);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_created ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_created ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_created ON orders (customer_id,created_at DESC)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_created ON orders (customer_id,created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_created ON orders(customer_id, created_at DESC)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_created ON orders(customer_id, created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_created ON orders(customer_id,created_at DESC)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_created ON orders(customer_id,created_at DESC);
questions.explanation: Equality column first, then the sort column: (customer_id, created_at). The database jumps to customer 42 and reads that customer's rows already in date order (it can walk the index backward for DESC). The reverse order, (created_at, customer_id), cannot jump to one customer.

questions.question: You index `countries(code)`, but EXPLAIN on `SELECT * FROM countries WHERE code = 'FR'` still shows a Seq Scan. The table has 250 rows. Why?
choices: The index is corrupted and must be rebuilt
For a tiny table, a sequential scan is cheaper than going through an index
New indexes are only used after a database restart
EXPLAIN always reports a Seq Scan, whatever really happens
questions.explanation: The planner estimates costs. A 250-row table fits in a page or two, so reading it straight through is cheaper than walking an index and then fetching rows. On a big table the same query would use the index.

questions.question: Type the statement that shows PostgreSQL's chosen plan for `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42` without running the query.
questions.answer: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
accept: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id=42
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id=42;
questions.explanation: Plain EXPLAIN shows the planned steps and estimates without executing. EXPLAIN ANALYZE would run the query and add real timings.

questions.question: To check its speed, you run this on production. What happens?
questions.code: EXPLAIN ANALYZE DELETE FROM sessions WHERE expires_at < now();
choices: The plan is shown with timings, and the matching rows really are deleted
Only the plan is shown; nothing is deleted
The statement is rejected, because EXPLAIN cannot be used with DELETE
The rows are deleted, but no timings are shown
questions.explanation: ANALYZE executes the statement to measure it, so the rows really are deleted. To measure a write safely, wrap it: BEGIN; EXPLAIN ANALYZE ...; ROLLBACK;

questions.question: Put these steps for fixing a slow query in a sensible order.
items: Capture the exact slow query and typical parameters
Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on production-sized data
Find the expensive step, such as a Seq Scan that discards most rows
Add or change an index that matches the filter and sort
Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE again and compare the timings
questions.explanation: Measure before you change anything, change one thing, then measure again. Adding indexes by guesswork without a plan to compare is how teams end up with dozens of unused indexes.

questions.question: Match each ACID property to what it guarantees.

pairs.right: All statements in the transaction take effect, or none do
Constraints such as foreign keys and CHECK rules hold after every commit
Concurrent transactions do not see each other's unfinished work
Committed data survives a crash or power loss

questions.explanation: Atomicity is all or nothing, consistency keeps constraints true, isolation hides unfinished work from other transactions, and durability keeps committed data after a crash.

questions.question: Match each concurrency anomaly to its description.

pairs.right: Reading another transaction's change before it commits, and it then rolls back
Reading the same row twice and getting two different committed values
Re-running a range query and seeing newly inserted rows
Two read-modify-write cycles overwrite each other and one change disappears

questions.explanation: Dirty reads see uncommitted data, non-repeatable reads see a row change between two reads, phantoms are new rows appearing in a repeated range query, and lost updates come from two read-modify-write cycles racing.

questions.question: Both updates succeeded. Complete the transaction so the transfer becomes permanent.
choices: ROLLBACK
SAVEPOINT
COMMIT
CHECKPOINT
questions.explanation: COMMIT makes every change since BEGIN permanent and visible to others. ROLLBACK would undo them, SAVEPOINT only marks a point inside the transaction, and CHECKPOINT is a maintenance command unrelated to your transaction.

questions.question: Halfway through a transaction you realize your UPDATE hit the wrong rows. Type the statement that undoes everything since BEGIN.
accept: ROLLBACK
ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;
ROLLBACK TRANSACTION
ROLLBACK WORK;
ROLLBACK WORK
ABORT;
ABORT
questions.explanation: ROLLBACK discards every change in the current transaction. This is why it is worth running risky manual updates inside BEGIN: you can check the result before deciding.

questions.question: Two withdrawals of 30 run at the same moment against a balance of 100, each in its own transaction at READ COMMITTED. The final balance is 70, not 40. What is the bug?
questions.code:
def withdraw(conn, account_id, amount):
    with conn:                       # one transaction
        cur = conn.cursor()
        cur.execute("SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = %s", (account_id,))
        balance = cur.fetchone()[0]
        if balance < amount:
            raise ValueError("insufficient funds")
        cur.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = %s WHERE id = %s",
                    (balance - amount, account_id))
choices: The %s placeholders make this query open to SQL injection
fetchone() returns the wrong row when two requests run at once
Both transactions read 100 before either writes, so one write overwrites the other; lock the row or use an atomic UPDATE
The with block commits after each statement instead of at the end
questions.explanation: Both transactions read 100 before either writes. Each computes 70 and writes it, so one withdrawal is lost. Lock the row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or do it in one atomic statement: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - %s WHERE id = %s AND balance >= %s, then check the row count.

questions.question: Under PostgreSQL's default isolation level, READ COMMITTED, which of these can still happen inside one transaction?
choices: Reading another transaction's uncommitted changes
Committed data disappearing after a crash
Reading the same row twice and getting different committed values
A foreign key violation being committed
questions.explanation: READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads, but each statement sees whatever was committed when it started, so two reads of the same row can differ. Lost committed data and committed constraint violations are prevented by durability and consistency at every level.

questions.question: Your development SQL log shows this for one page load. What is the problem, and what is the fix?
questions.code:
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' LIMIT 50
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = 7
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = 9
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = 12
... 47 more queries like these
choices: A missing index on orders.status; add one
An N+1 pattern; load the customers with the orders in one JOIN or one IN query
The LIMIT is too small; raise it to 500
The customers table must be merged into orders
questions.explanation: One query for the list plus one per row is the N+1 pattern. Load the customers together with the orders, through a JOIN (select_related, joinedload) or one IN query (prefetch_related, selectinload).

questions.question: A page lists 40 posts and shows each post's author name. The code loads the posts, then reads `post.author.name` in a loop with no eager loading. How many queries run?
questions.explanation: One query loads the 40 posts, then each of the 40 posts triggers its own author query: 1 + 40 = 41. Eager loading brings it down to 1 or 2.

questions.question: What is the vulnerability in this search endpoint?
choices: SQL injection: the search term becomes part of the SQL text, so crafted input changes the query
LIKE patterns cannot contain the % character
fetchall() returns every table in the database
jsonify turns the rows into executable SQL
questions.explanation: The search term is pasted into the SQL text, so an input such as `' OR 1=1 --` rewrites the query. Pass it as a parameter instead: `db.execute("SELECT id, title FROM posts WHERE title LIKE ?", (f"%{term}%",))`.

questions.question: Complete the call so `email` is passed safely as a bound parameter with Python's sqlite3.
questions.code: cur.execute("SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = ?", _____)
choices: (email)
(email,)
f"{email}"
questions.explanation: Parameters go in a sequence, and a one-element tuple needs the trailing comma: (email,). Plain (email) is just a string in parentheses, so sqlite3 complains about the number of bindings. Gluing quotes or using an f-string reintroduces injection.

questions.question: Users can sort a product list by a column they choose. A teammate writes `cur.execute("SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY %s", (sort,))`. Why does this not work as intended?
choices: %s only works for numbers, so sort must be converted with int()
Placeholders bind values, not identifiers, so a column name cannot be passed this way; use an allowlist of column names
ORDER BY cannot be used together with any parameters in the same query
It works fine, because a parameter can replace any part of a query
questions.explanation: Bound parameters are always treated as values, never as column or table names. Depending on the database you get an error or a sort by a constant string. Map the user's choice through an allowlist such as {'price': 'price_cents', 'newest': 'created_at DESC'} and insert only your own text.

questions.question: Which of these are good fits for a key-value store such as Redis? Select all that apply.
choices: Session data looked up by session id
Per-user rate-limit counters that reset every minute
A cache of rendered product pages keyed by URL
Monthly revenue reports joining orders, refunds and customers
A payments ledger that must satisfy foreign key constraints
questions.explanation: Sessions, counters and caches are all 'get or set by key, often with expiry', which is what key-value stores do best. Ad hoc reports with joins and ledgers with cross-row rules need a relational database.

questions.question: Which workload fits a document database best?
choices: Double-entry bookkeeping across thousands of accounts
Weekly reports that join five tables in new ways
Bank transfers that must update two accounts atomically
A product catalog where each product has different attributes and is read as a whole
questions.explanation: A catalog where each product has its own set of attributes and is read as one unit is the textbook document-store case. Bookkeeping, atomic transfers and changing multi-table reports lean on joins, constraints and transactions, which relational databases do best.
